slides.page_title: Approximated LRU: The 24-Bit Clock and Sample Pool

items: True LRU needs a doubly-linked list touched on every access.
That is extra pointers per object plus cache-hostile chasing.
Redis refuses to pay it and approximates instead.
Each `robj` carries a 24-bit coarse clock: Unix seconds, truncated.
24 bits of seconds wraps every ~194 days.
Comparison code handles wraparound; idle time is modulo that range.
`LRU_CLOCK_RESOLUTION` = 1000 ms.

blocks.title: No syscall per access
blocks.text: The clock is read from a cached global that `serverCron` updates — never `gettimeofday` on the hot path.

items: Eviction samples `maxmemory-samples` random keys, default 5.
It evicts the one with the oldest clock value.
Redis 3.0 added a 16-entry pool of the best candidates so far.
The pool is refilled each round, so good victims survive passes.

blocks.title: Highest-value LRU knob
blocks.text: `CONFIG SET maxmemory-samples 10`. Measure hit ratio before and after — do not raise it past that on faith.

items: ==Idle time== = LRU clock now minus the key's stored clock.
Resolution is one second — sub-second recency is invisible.
High idle time marks the next likely **victim**.
Track `evicted_keys` rate beside the ==hit ratio==.
Rising evictions + falling hits = cache too **small**.
Tune samples only after sizing `maxmemory` correctly.

lines: OBJECT IDLETIME user:42   # seconds since access
# meaningful only under an LRU policy
# DEBUG paths do not count as an access here

blocks.title: Sampling cost is eviction-only
blocks.text: Extra samples are paid when a victim is chosen, never on reads — so the knob barely touches normal latency.

slides.page_title: LRU's Scan Blind Spot and the LFU Morris Counter

items: One scan job touches everything once and evicts your hot set.
A `KEYS`-style traversal or big `MGET` sweep does exactly this.
That failure has a name: scan resistance failure.
LRU also cannot tell 'once, recently' from '10,000 times, recently'.

blocks.title: Shared bits, shared machinery
items: `volatile-ttl` reuses the pool, ranking by nearest deadline.
Under LFU the same 24 bits mean counter + timestamp.
You get recency or frequency, never both.
`utils/lru/test-lru.rb` renders true vs approximated victims.
Added in Redis 4.0 to answer LRU's weakness.
An item hit thousands of times should outrank one hit ten seconds ago.
Recency alone throws that history away.
16 bits: last-decrement time, in minutes.
8 bits: a logarithmic access counter.
8 bits cannot hold a real count, so the counter is probabilistic.
It is a Morris counter — approximate by construction.

lines: # fast at first, then slower and slower

items: New keys start at `LFU_INIT_VAL` = 5, not 0.
So a fresh key gets a chance to prove itself first.
Otherwise every new key would be the instant next victim.

blocks.title: Lazy decay is free
blocks.text: No background pass walks the keyspace to age counters, so an idle instance spends nothing on LFU bookkeeping.

slides.page_title: LFU Decay: Lazy Aging and the Minute Clock

items: Without decay, yesterday's hot key stays untouchable forever.
So the counter is halved or decremented over time.
`lfu-decay-time` (default 1) = minutes of idleness per step down.
Decay is lazy: applied on next touch or sample, never swept.
The 16-bit ==minute clock== wraps every ~45 days.
Wraparound is handled like the LRU clock, modulo the range.
Counter never drops below 0; a cold key becomes the **victim**.

blocks.title: Two dials, two jobs
blocks.text: `lfu-log-factor` shapes how fast counters climb; `lfu-decay-time` shapes how fast they forget.

blocks.title: Scan resistance
blocks.text: A one-pass batch job leaves counters near 5, so its keys go first and your hot set survives. LRU cannot do this.

items: Per-access work is the same as LRU: one field update.
The trade-off is tuning complexity, not throughput.
Failure mode: a real traffic shift promotes slowly.
New feature or new tenant slow to warm? Shorten `lfu-decay-time`.

blocks.title: Comparison row to memorise
items: LRU: recency, 1 knob, loses to scans.
LFU: frequency + decay, 3 knobs, resists scans.
LFU adapts slowly to genuine shifts.
AOF never records an expiry implicitly.
Expiry and eviction are both written as real commands.
So AOF replay is deterministic, not clock-dependent.

blocks.title: Failover hazard
blocks.text: After promotion, a replica's own clock and its inherited-but-unexpired keys govern. Large skew between nodes changes what is visible.

lines: # fires on reclamation, not on the deadline

blocks.title: Safer than expiry events
items: `ZADD jobs <deadline> id` per job.
Poll `ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs -inf <now>`.
`ZREM` the id, then run it — you own the timing.

slides.page_title: Expiry Event Limits and Related Keys in a Cluster

items: Delay between deadline and event is unbounded.
Delivery is pub/sub: fire-and-forget, no persistence.
Never build a job scheduler on it alone.
Cluster: keys expire per shard, so related keys never expire together.

slides.page_title: Gotchas, Persistence, and the Cheat Sheet

items: `SET` after `EXPIRE` clears the TTL — the key goes immortal.
`EXPIRE` on every `INCR` slides the rate-limit window forever.
`volatile-lru` with no TTLs anywhere: OOM on an 'evictable' instance.
Assuming a TTL frees memory on time — reclamation is only 'soon'.
Uniform TTLs: synchronised expiry, CPU spike, replication burst, stampede.
Treating `DBSIZE` as authoritative — it counts logically-expired keys.
And it differs between primary and replica by design.

lines: SET sess:1 v2           # wrong: immortal now
EXPIRE sess:1 60 GT     # right: extend only

items: Budget: `maxmemory`, `maxmemory-policy`, `maxmemory-samples`.
LFU: `lfu-log-factor`, `lfu-decay-time`.
Expiry rate: `hz`, `dynamic-hz`.
Latency: `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `activedefrag`.

blocks.title: The whole handbook in one line
blocks.text: TTLs make keys invisible on time and reclaimed approximately; `maxmemory` turns approximate reclamation into a hard budget; LRU and LFU are both sampled guesses, tuned by `maxmemory-samples` and the two `lfu-*` dials.

a_bullets: `maxmemory` set, policy matched to the workload.
TTLs jittered; `KEEPTTL` audited on every overwrite path.
Eviction counters on a dashboard before traffic arrives.

caption.text: Part 2 of REDIS EXPIRY & EVICTION. Your Redis key did not disappear at its deadline — it just became invisible. This handbook walks the whole death pipeline: the TTL command surface and the flags that quietly clear it, the lazy and active expiry cycles that actually reclaim memory, and how maxmemory turns 'soon' into a hard budget under approximated LRU and LFU. Ten pages of internals, sampling math, and the six mistakes that cause silent data loss or an OOM at 3am.
